title: Solid Fool’s Gold
author: Bill James

mentions.title: Solid Fool’s Gold
mentions.context: Solid Fool’s Gold, James 2011 Solid Fool’s Gold: Detours on the Way to Conventional WisdomBill James2011★★☆☆☆ Downloaded for forgotten reasons, finally got around to it as some light bedtime reading. Baseball is not one of my favorite sports, to say the least; I can enjoy basketball a little bit, and football (as long as there is an “all 20” or equivalent view, otherwise football makes no sense to me), I’ve done enough soccer and martial arts to enjoy watching those briefly, and probably my most memorable sports experience was a high school NY state championship match where all 100 spectators on both sides lept to their feet when after a mad dash down the rink our team scored the winning goal with a second on the clock. But baseball? Baseball is not just boring, it is quite possibly the most boring popular sport in the world. That is probably why it is so parochial, and has so signally failed to spread globally (baseball is played only in the USA and former colonies thereof), people use baseball soundtracks to fall asleep, baseball writers shamefacedly admit that it’s hard to write anything interesting about it & wrap themselves in pretzels explaining why being boring is great, the MLB is forced to experiment with a load of tweaks to make it less boring & cope with competition from actually-interesting sports like basketball, and one of the hottest baseball trends is to avoid having to watch baseball & instead gamble on it; one statistical analysis politely phrases it as baseball games having “the highest percentage of game segments that are played in less competitive situations”. (Tom Brady was an even better baseball player than football player as a youth, but chose football because he “always liked football once he started playing”, which sounds to me like a polite way of saying baseball was boring.) After attending 3–5 Mets, Yankees, and Long Island Ducks games (in addition to being forced to attend any number of Little League games and the occasional amateur game in Boy Scouts or school), I can safely say that I would prefer to sit on the floor in an empty room watching paint dry—as it would be quieter, the food probably better and cheap, the seat more comfortable, and hey, I could practice meditating. But, Bill James is the godfather of the ‘sabermetrics’ or ‘moneyball’ revolution and I am constantly hearing him invoked as an example of how hardheaded statistical analysis can undermine decade or century-old conventional wisdom, and I thought perhaps I could learn something about applied statistics from him. And a good writer or analyst makes any subject interesting, as Nate Silver did so well in The Signal and the Noise. I was not impressed. James’s ramblings on non-statistical topics are typically not well-reasoned/supported, like his rant against tipping (outlawed? good luck with that), or are unfunny (did anyone laugh at “Olympic NASCAR Racing”?), or that advertising will collapse (you’d’ve made a lot of money in stocks since 201115ya if you’d negated James’s predictions). James’s suggestion of a rainfall unit of “inches per time”, on the other hand, is a genuinely useful suggestion… so useful that it’s already a meteorology unit, since replaced by “millimeters per hour” (which you measure with a pluviometer). Some of them were mildly interesting, like “Justice McReynolds and Buck O’Neil”. A relatively sports-free essay, “Shakespeare and Verlander: Why are we so good at developing athletes and so lousy at developing writers?” is good, but makes a point made elsewhere by a number of people like Charles Murray and in any case, I’d already read it back in 201115ya on Slate. Some of the baseball ones are too inside-baseball for me to judge. There is surely someone for whom “The 33 Greatest Starting Rotations of All-Time In Chronological Order Apropos of Nothing in Particular”, a long list of tables with brief comments, is interesting, though they are not me. “The Expansion Bomb” sounds like it might be interesting but we are in the middle of said “bomb” and if Baseball Hall of Fame elections have caused major controversy due to changing standards over time, the furor has not reached my ears. The most striking part of his baseball analyses is what he didn’t write: about steroid abuse, of which BALCO was but the tip of the iceberg. (Was James unable to see what countless people saw without need of statistics, and which jumped out in the statistical anomalies that set countless headlines in the home run races, or was he just too cowardly to write about it?) The statistics left me even less impressed. James says he’s not a statistician… and it shows. The sabermetrics on display seems more like a child’s idea of what statistics is (long tabulations of data fed into simple arithmetic formulas to generate yet more tabulations of ‘variables’) than what it really is (quantitative modeling of the world and decision-making under uncertainty). His modus operandi seems to be to just pull some number or formula out of his nether regions by arbitrarily weighting some other variables after slicing them up (eg. the “Stink-O-Meter”) and then give some anecdotes involving that made-up variable. I would be thrilled to see some real statistics like linear regression, or maybe even factor analysis for dimensionality reduction (instead of arbitrarily deciding to weight one variable 0.25 and another two variables 0.375 etc.), but realistically, James would benefit from doing anything which would test his made-up numbers. He has many easy ways to do better—he doesn’t have to be a hardcore statistician building elaborate Bayesian models with custom MCMC routines (although that would be nice and he could’ve easily started doing so in the 1990s). For example, given his large tabular datasets, resampling (eg. for permutation testing) is about as simple a concept as could be, is dead easy to program (even into a 1980s spreadsheet by shuffling rows/columns), and would clarify a lot about whether his formulas predict at all or correlate out of sample or are accidents or even statistically-significant given the very complicated sampling distribution of professional baseball. And yet, he’s done next to not nothing all these years. He’s certainly had enough time to up his game! One 198343ya article, “The Law of Competitive Advantage”, struck me as bafflingly bad (and perhaps exemplifying why James should try to identify a little more as a statistician). In this article, James waxes at length about phenomena such as how teams which are losing can come back, and how teams which are winning often fall back or lose, elevating this observation to ‘the law of competitive advantage’. Well, it’s a law, alright—a statistical law. Could Bill James have seriously made a career of analyzing a competitive sport and not know what “regression to the mean” is‽ I kept waiting for the punchline where he revealed that these cute stories about all these ‘laws’ and ‘Plexiglas principle’ and ‘whirlpool principle’ and whatnot are in fact all manifestations of one and the same principle, and the reader, having been fooled by some plausible storytelling, would do well to remember that any time we talk about a subset like ‘winning teams’ or ‘top players’ we are inherently talking about a selection effect which will create regression to a mean and need not invoke any fancy dynamics beyond ordinary randomness, and… it never came. He does append one odd footnote: I have no doubt, 28 years later, that the ‘separate and unequal strategies’ distinction that I drew here is real, and I could cite now many, many more studies in which this has been evident. However, the tendency of teams to move toward the center is caused by this phenomenon and by many other causes. I should have been more clear about that. This is not an anomaly, as he deploys a similar rhetorical strategy in a 2022 article, prompting a critical post by Andrew Gelman, where he acknowledges an unspecified criticism sent to him by a reader about how his batting example is an statistical artifact—so the reader in question almost certainly brought up regression to a mean, specifically—and then proceeding to deny that such effects exist at all, and claiming his competitive advantage/plexiglas/whirlpool stuff are all the real deal! Er, what? This borders on intellectual dishonesty—assuming James is in fact referring to the observation that regression to a mean amply accounts for most/all of his findings (his defensive footnote is so oblique I cannot be sure he is), he ought to either not select as one of his best pieces for republishing, fix his analysis to demonstrate which (if any) of his findings are more than merely regression to a mean and publish that instead, or be honest with the reader and explain what regression to a mean is & why it can explain all of his findings & why he nevertheless intuitively believes they are not entirely regression to a mean. Yes, James, you should have been more clear about that, then—and now. But you don’t even mention what those ‘many other causes are’! If only you were a rich successful author publishing decades later, at leisure, a bunch of your best writings in some new anthology, which would allow you to edit the article to fix it and let you be clearer about things… If only. Ultimately, I was not amused and learned nothing from James’s entire book (except perhaps another case-study of how regression to a mean can fool people). To the extent James deserves a reputation as an influential impartial analyst of sports statistics, it seems it is only because he was the least incompetent & biased analyst writing publicly at the time. Anti-recommended to all non-sabermetricians (and even those should think twice as I am left in considerable doubt about the quality of James’s analyses).

title: Existence
author: David Brin

mentions.title: Existence
mentions.context: Existence, Brin 2012 ExistenceDavid Brin2012★★☆☆☆ Existence is best-seen as a rewrite of Earth, and Earth was a sprawling futurological serious novel which was trying to both world-build by including countless perspectives and quotes and discussions and terms but also put them into context to build a overarching thesis. Similar to Tad William’s Otherland trilogy (the good first book City of Golden Shadow, not the bad sequels), Dos Passos’s U.S.A., or particularly Brunner’s Stand On Zanzibar (to which Brin alludes, actually, in having an alien say “what an imagination I’ve got.”) The overriding theme is, of course, the Great Silence. Brin’s solution, characteristically for a guy who wants to be the ultimate moderate and more moderate than thou, is to endorse every solution: the Great Silence is due to more efficient physical transportation and memetic viruses and Berserkers and Lurkers and panspermia and ecological collapse and nuclear war and… This is a little impressive to behold, and overall, I did enjoy reading the book. Brin has had a few new ideas since Earth like the smart-mob. But for the bad: This jumping makes the book something like a huge primer on the Great Silence/Fermi’s Question, yes, but also for something of a mess of a book. The book is huge, but a good deal of the bulk is fat and self-indulgent: the dolphin sub-plot is rehashed Uplift material, which only very charitably has any relevance to anything else in the book (I thought that we would at least see them towards the end on spaceships as a token nod toward justifying the time spent on them, but no!) More germane subplots feel incomplete; the autistic kids, “cobblies” and the “Basque Chimera” form one such oddly underjustified subplot—is this a thing, now, lauding crippled autistic kids as secret savant heroes? I don’t know which narrative is more denigrating of the human suffering involved, the standard one or this one. (Autism spectrum may be useful in some areas, but only a little is necessary and even the high-functioning often fail: I read in the New York Times the other day that that famous tech firm which uses autistic workers has a 5⁄6 rejection rate of applicants just from the start. One must sift a lot of sand.) Stale sense. much material is borrowed from his previous nonfiction or fiction; allusions to The Postman are well and good, but when I could predict the resolution of the Senator Strong mystery from the instant we were told it was an addiction… This also means that I can track how many authorial mouthpieces there are in the novel, and it’s pretty much all of them. Even people you think are wrong like Hamish are just acting as conduits for Brin’s own beliefs. This leads to the severe problem, in a (repeated) first contact novel, that none of the aliens were remotely alien, and the humans all seemed pretty similar to each other too. It made me wish for Stanislaw Lem, or at least Peter Watts’s Blindsight. New nonsense. Brin also has a very weird attitude towards what he calls extropianism but most people these days just call transhumanism. For example, the bogus anti-caloric restriction argument a character gives to the effect that “we know caloric restriction can’t help because many monks in history reduced their food and didn’t live longer”; it is bogus because (a) none of those monks or monasteries are following nutritionally balanced diets, indeed, usually for religious reasons they’re following highly unbalanced diets if they’re not like the Taoists possibly actively poisoning themselves with mercury, and (b) those monks do, in fact, claim countless instances of extreme longevity—which of course we don’t believe because record-keeping was terrible—which then means the evidence is so worthless and biased and corrupt that we can’t use it to claim the opposite either! (Any monk who claimed to have lived longer than Jeanne Calment, and was right, would, unfortunately, just be a baby in a lot of bathwater.) I’ve told Brin this before, not that he cared. But by the time the story is set, the caloric restriction question will be settled: the primate studies will be finished, the human CRers will be dead, and the underlying biochemistry (or lack thereof) will be known. Suppose he’s wrong? He probably doesn’t care, he’s dead-set against it anyway! I was a little awe-struck when he has his mouthpiece badmouth cryonics, after saying it worked and there had been revivals? WTF? WTF indeed. This attitude could be called schizophrenic. Struggling with Singularities. Throughout the novel, Brin seems to struggle with the fundamental problem posed by Vinge: how does he keep the story human given his belief in progress and his basic acceptance of the Strong AI thesis?16 He never comes up with a good answers, but blatantly hand-waves them away: an emulated rat brain goes critical and escapes into the Internet? Well, uh—nothing happens because I say so (wow, ain’t it strange)! There are even more AIs pervading the world, controlling countless key functions? Well, uh—nothing happens because I insinuate something about parents and children and them being grateful! (wow, ain’t it strange—ever see a grateful river, spider, tow-truck, computer…? Humans can barely be grateful, ever.) Humanity is a few decades away from a general nanofactory assembler in his story and thousands of crystal probes come to visit? Well, uh—the crystal probes are completely inactive and don’t carry nanofactories or anything despite it being a mindbogglingly great & evolutionarily fit idea and perfectly doable for them, because I say so and it lets me write adventure arcs with primates fighting over & chucking around glowing rocks! (wow, ain’t it strange.) He’ll mock the extropians in the first part for believing in cryonics or uploads or AIs even though their most-criticized belief, cryonics, has been vindicated 100% in his story even beyond their hopes, their expectations of uploads are equally justified by events towards the end—non-destructive uploading, even! We’d settle for destructive uploads at this point… and so on and so forth. Well, uh—they’re right but they’re wrong, don’t you see! (wow, ain’t it strange.) Brin as public intellectual. Brin was omnipresent in the 1990s and early 2000s, and made major contributions with his mailing list, early-adopting blog-like articles (for Salon.com especially), books like The Transparent Society (199828ya); someone who read that and then Kiln People (200224ya) not long after would have expected great things from an author who had found a centrist niche and successfully emigrated to the Internet & what we’d call social media, and was writing a successful blog (which remarkably, he continues to write). But those were the high-water mark: Brin’s output over the 2000s just got worse and worse, as he turned into a hectoring Democrat partisan barely above the level of a Daily Kos or AlterNet blogger. I had been a mailing list participant & blog subscriber for years, but somewhere around 201016ya, I think, I simply dropped it. Not because I disagreed on much substantive grounds, but because intellectually, there was nothing left but a dry husk, sucked dry by politics. I have every few years checked in on his blog to see how he is doing, and every time I am astounded how he appears to be trapped in amber—for example, the first sentence when I checked in 2019 was “The Handmaid’s Tale, Putin-led putsch hasn’t won yet!”; I check in on his blog today, 2022-10-06, and the first post is filled with exactly the same Boomer and Brinisms as 200917ya, about how Brin is the best predictor in the world, the Republican Party the worst thing in the world, and even the same talking points about government budgets I remember from the mid-2000s when he couldn’t stop ranting about the George W. Bush tax cuts. Existence: an epitaph. Existence can be seen as the ebb-mark where his political turn, having apparently neutered his fiction output for a decade, turned out to have compromised his fiction because it was just bad—the good in it is cribbed from decades before, and the new in it is outrageously unfair or peevishly nonsensical. (One way of marking Brin’s decline is to simply note that Kiln People is his last major work which, as of 2022, has a Wikipedia article on it.) It did reasonably well because recycled-good-Brin is still decent, especially if you don’t think too hard about the bad parts or don’t recognize the targets or copied parts, but it’s telling that after it, Brin has disappeared from the geek Internet zeitgeist. Rise & fall. In this trajectory, Brin resembles another liberal writer of that era, Paul Krugman, albeit Krugman has been in worldly terms rewarded in proportion to the loss of quality. (Before there was “Trump derangement syndrome”, there was George W. Bush derangement syndrome.) Both are a cautionary lesson for any writers or public intellectuals: politics can be a useful servant, but is a tyrant as master, which will burn you out and sacrifice all your good qualities, and desires nothing more than to render you a mind-killed squawking mouth of outrage. Explore vs exploit. The ‘curse of the public intellectual’ is to draw on a store they husbanded over decades, and then spend it prodigally in the public eye, while forgetting that to reap those rewards now, they must have sown before. And the nature of politics is that it is the thinking-man’s sportsball in providing an infinite amount of randomized topics to comment about every day in an unmindful fashion: did you hear about the latest outrage? Oh, there wasn’t one today? No problem, we collectively (and loonies specifically) will manufacture a new one to fill the void. And then you look up, and a decade has passed, and you have nothing to show for it but a pile of blog posts on ‘scandals’ now more forgotten than the proverbial “Schleswig-Holstein question”, or ‘receipts’ & ‘dunks’ whose rush of sadistic pleasure quickly turned as vile in the stomach as eating pounds of candy on Halloween. (Most political involvement is better analogized to masturbation than cogitation—pleasurable, presumably, but not productive, except of byproducts to be discarded down the drain without a second glance.) RIP. “Whatever happened to X?” people will wonder. It’s not hard to explain; what happened to him was precisely what it looked like. He has become embittered, and gone stale as he failed to reinvent himself, or replenish the wellsprings of his mind. (What has post-2009 Krugman done worth remembering?) As an intellectual, he is dead, whether or not he has bothered with the formality of physical death, and so everyone moves on.

metadata.title: The Postman
metadata.author: David Brin
metadata.description: This is the story of a lie that became the most powerful kind of truth.  A timeless novel as urgently compelling as War Day or Alas, Babylon, David Brin's The Postman is the dramatically moving saga of a man who rekindled the spirit of America through the power of a dream, from a modern master of science fiction.He was a survivor--a wanderer who traded tales for food and shelter in the dark and savage aftermath of a devastating war.  Fate touches him one chill winter's day when he borrows the jacket of a long-dead postal worker to protect himself from the cold.  The old, worn uniform still has power as a symbol of hope, and with it he begins to weave his greatest tale, of a nation on the road to recovery.From the Paperback edition.

mentions.title: Machine Super Intelligence
mentions.context: Overall, I would absolutely recommend against this book for any laymen interested in statistics or machine learning. The explanations are so poor and garbled that you will either not learn anything or what you take away will be as likely to be misleading as not. You will be better off with Silver’s The Signal and the Noise, reading random presentations on Schmidhuber’s website, Bostrom’s Superintelligence or even Hutter’s Machine Super Intelligence or Domingos’s own “A Few Useful Things to Know about Machine Learning” (which was really good) or anything really. (Suggestions are welcomed on things I can recommend for laymen instead of this…)

title: Fascinating Mathematical People
author: Donald J. Albers and Gerald L. Alexanderson

mentions.title: Fascinating Mathematical People
mentions.context: Fascinating Mathematical People, Albers 2011 Fascinating Mathematical People: Interviews and MemoirsDonald J. Albers2011★★☆☆☆ Interviews with 16 mathematicians 1990–20201016ya, similar to the earlier volume Mathematical People (see my review of it). I don’t recognize any of the interviewees: Ahlfors, Apostol, Bacon, Banchoff, Bankoff, Beckenbach, Benjamin, Cartwright, Gallian, Guy, Hunt, McDuff, Saari, Selberg, Taylor, Tondeur. On the whole, I found this volume far less interesting than the other collection. Most of the subjects are post-WWII, non-European (certainly not part of the fascinatingly aristocratic-but-democratic pre-war European mathematical communities), and their lives come off as colorless beneficiaries of the post-WWII expansion of higher ed, moving fairly easily from undergrad to grad to tenure. The interviewers don’t have as much personal connection to the interviewees. The exceptions are not always pleasant to read about; Ahlfors, a Finn who had made his way to the USA before WWII, recounts how he patriotically moved himself and his family back to Finland, contributed zilch to the war effort, and then had to place himself and his family at great risk in getting back out of Europe, the sort of story one expects to end with “and then 15 years later, their remains were discovered in a shallow grave near the main road” (meanwhile, I am thinking “you stupid Finn—you went back? You would have helped infinitely more if you had stayed back in the USA or UK!”) Few of them can claim to be nearly as colorful as Conway or Diaconis etc., and there’s a really striking absence of computers or statistics or anything you might call application. (I think there is one meaningful mention of computers, in the context of computing many zeros of the Riemann function as a heuristic argument for it being true.) This is particularly astonishing given the time period they were interviewed over. I also think that the earlier interviews did better jobs of explaining their professional topics than these do; how they manage the trick of simultaneously being boring or uninformative about the people and being boring or uninformative about their work too, I am not sure. I think they may simply be much shorter but I haven’t done a word-count. The interviews are not 100% rubbish, though. Guy and Selberg make some interesting remarks. Saari is quite amusing. Joseph Gallian’s interview paints a memorable picture of union factory work and the occupational hazards which frightened him into mathematics. Dusa McDuff had both a somewhat unusual life and an interesting grandmother. Other than that Overall, the selection of interviews gave me an impression that in some respects, these were the leftovers. To be read only if one is already interested in one of the interviewees.

title: Soldiers Live

mentions.title: Soldiers Live
mentions.context: Soldiers Live, Cook 2001 Soldiers Live (The Chronicles of the Black Company, #9)Glen Cook2001★★☆☆☆ A weirdly quiet and sedate ending to the entire series. It’s great that we have Croaker back so the series begins as it ended, but the plot is just too odd and incomplete. Everything happens too easily—I began worrying as I started the book, there were too many loose ends and nothing set up for a grand ending, and that’s exactly what happened. We have the Black Company at the start overpowered as usual, as it has since Smoky started napping, with the further assistance of an even more overpowered demon; they slice through resistance with the greatest of ease, enemies like Soulcatcher or Booboo or Goblin go down trivially, and even the final defeat of Kina comes as trivial anticlimax (how the deuce did it make a lick of sense that the ancient gods couldn’t destroy Kina if a little hedge wizard’s spear and an exploding airplane can do the trick‽). The ‘twist’ ending is not shocking or compelling, and my reaction was ‘oh. Well, that’s nice for Croaker, I guess.’ I’m sure there’s all good explanations in-universe along the lines of ‘the demon was helping them the entire time and eg. that’s why the forvalaka dies so easily’, but an explanation is just an explanation and it doesn’t rescue a bad story. I’m left just shaking my head, wondering what went wrong. Why did Cook go to such lengths to introduce a character as powerful and hence game-breaking as Tobo while implying a narrative of power-corrupts which never goes anywhere besides one or two instances of revenge? Why did he make the demon so cooperative? Why did he make the Howler die, in what must be the only instance in the entire damn series where a Taken dies and stays dead‽ And so on and so forth. Reading through some interviews with Cook, I find myself wondering if he just wanted to stop the series and didn’t really try hard on the ending—he certainly comes off as cynical and mercenary about writing, with little of Croaker’s faith in the power of the Annals. Looking back, many of the books in The Black Company were weak enough that I can’t really blame him for intending to stop with the first one, but now that I’m done, I’m not sure I’ll bother with any future books in the universe (apparently he has one or two in the pipeline). Although the title is excellent and used well.

mentions.title: The Legend of Sigurd and Gudrún
mentions.context: The Legend of Sigurd and Gudrún, Tolkien 2009 The Legend of Sigurd and GudrúnJ. R. R. Tolkien2009★★☆☆☆ The essential problem with this book is that the Norse wonk will already know most of the background, and the actual poetry is incredibly padded out, with ridiculous amounts of whitespace which badly interfere with reading. As quixotic as attempting to write alliterative verse in modern English may seem, Tolkien has some marvelous verses that work. For example: The Great Gods then || began their toil, the wondrous world || they well builded. From South the Sun || from seas rising gleamed down on grass || green at morning. They hall and hallow || high uptowering, gleaming-gabled, || golden-posted, rock-hewn ramparts || reared in splendour, forge and fortress || framed immortal. Or: The falls of Andvari || frothed and murmured with fish teeming || in foaming pools. As pike there plunged || his prey hunting Dwarf Andvari || from his dark cavern. There hunted hungry || Hreidmar’s offspring: the silver salmon || sweet he thought them. Otr in otter’s form || there ate blinking on the bank brooding || of black waters. Or: At the dark doorways || they dinned and hammered; there was clang of swords || and crash of axes. The smiths of battle || smote the anvils; sparked and splintered || spears and helmets. In they hacked them, || out they hurled them, bears assailing, || boars defending. Stones and stairways || streamed and darkened; day came dimly— || the doors were held. But for the most part, the verse is something of a chore to get through. Heaney’s Beowulf may not be as good at alliterative verse as the best of Tolkien’s here, but Tolkien is worse on average.

title: Tales of Ise
author: Helen Craig McCullough

mentions.title: Tales of Ise
mentions.context: Tales of Ise, Anonymous 1968 Tales of Ise: Lyrical Episodes from Tenth-Century JapanAnonymous1968★★☆☆☆ Tales of Ise is one of the acknowledged classics of ancient and medieval Japanese literature, cited or alluded to nearly as much as the Kokinshu, Tale of Genji, or Man’yoshu; Keene praises it in almost extravagant terms in Seeds in the Heart. It is an anthology of poems with snippets of prose context relating the circumstances, expansions of the notes often attached to poems explaining the context or topic. The stories are threadbare, stereotypical, and lacking in any kind of charm or characterization, and it is clear that few of them can claim any defense from the truth as they are so obviously made up to explain the poem (similar to the ‘just so’ etymologies/histories one seems in many religious texts or myths to explain place names) or are so vague as to be meaningless or seem highly improbable and unattested elsewhere (like sleeping with the priestess of Ise). Reading it was a chore, and McCullough’s translations manage to butcher poems I had loved in other translations; here, for example, is McCullough’s translation of one of Narihira’s most famous poems, on dying: This road, I have long been told, Man travels in the end— Yet I had not thought to go Yesterday or today. Yeah. The whole book is like that. I hope other translations are much better, but it is difficult for me to imagine that the substance of these stories, no matter how skilled the translator, could ever stand up to The Tale of Genji or even The Pillow Book of Sei Shonagon (which as harsh as I was on some aspects of it, overall was far better than this and more worthy of its repute).

mentions.context: The Mature Optimization Handbook, Bueno 2013 The Mature Optimization HandbookCarlos Bueno2013★★☆☆☆ TMOH is so short I am hesitant to call it a book or judge it by the standards of one (less than 90 pages excluding the wrappers), but considered as a book about computer optimization, it is weak and idiosyncratic, and is much less worth reading that Google’s SRE book (even though that is not primarily about optimization at all). TMOH is based primarily on Facebook/WWW programming topics, leading to odd focuses—for example, it’s hard to imagine that very many people need be deeply concerned about the dynamics of global load balancing DNS systems bouncing users to nearby datacenters or might run into the pathologies of not getting the update time window just right (ch12), or that one of the most important things a programmer needs to know about optimizing is how to generate text logs with a specific format and field like script_path (ch5). I get the impression that this might have originally been intended for getting Facebook interns up to speed on datacenter tweaking and then Bueno tried to expand it into a more general book, which would explain the awkwardness and why it can’t seem to decide whether it’s explaining a few of the odder nooks and crannies of Facebook’s hyperscale datacenters and PHP software stack or trying to describe how to debug and maintain a legacy system. I did enjoy some of the debugging war stories.

mentions.context: Puzzles of the Black Widowers, Asimov 1991 Puzzles of the Black Widowers (The Black Widowers, #5)Isaac Asimov1991★★☆☆☆ Pretty meh. Most of the puzzles turn on some ridiculous gimmick that no one but the author would ever think of, and the ones which don’t are dumb. (The most offensive one being the final stolen-recipe one, which is the worst ‘locked room’ mystery I’ve ever read—a recipe is stolen from a woman while she babysits a house of children. ‘I bet it was one of the kids’, I thought a third of the way through. It was. Even Isaac Asimov’s reputation couldn’t get some of these stinkers published before!) The only two I’d call actually good is “The Four-Leaf Clover” for its interesting little debate about exploiting the superstitious, and “Unique Is Where You Find It”, where Asimov shows off his knowledge of the periodic table by describing how almost every element has some way in which it can be considered unique (if he left out any, well, presumably that element is unique in being non-unique)!, which would make a nice little essay in its own right related to Occam’s razor and the underdetermination of theories by data. (Copies are available online. Download, don’t spend good money on this.)

title: Experimenter Effects In Behavioral Research
author: Robert Rosenthal

mentions.title: Experimenter Effects In Behavioral Research
mentions.context: Experimenter Effects In Behavioral Research, Rosenthal 1976 Experimenter Effects In Behavioral ResearchRobert Rosenthal1976★☆☆☆☆ (ebook) Review of a major and widely-cited psychology monograph purporting to demonstrate pervasive and powerful effects of social expectations and settings and the general environment on all aspects of human psychology, experimentation, and research, even to the point of the ‘Pygmalion effect’ proving that teacher expectations can boost student IQs by hundreds of points. The Pygmalion effect was based on impossible data, was defended by statistical malpractice, and repeatedly failed to replicate, and this exemplifies the problem with Rosenthal’s research and the book as a whole: despite its appearance of extreme rigor and concern for bias, it is clear that the results actually exemplify the Replication Crisis and that almost none of his research is reliable, bogus from beginning to end, and the results were designed to serve ideological goals despite the intrinsic absurdity of the claims, and inconsistency with basic observations of human stability & consistency, predictive power of individual differences, and impotence of environmental interventions. A 197551ya monograph by Robert Rosenthal on observer-related biases and influences on, primarily, humans, such as social status or self-fulfilling prophecies. Rosenthal is one of the most influential psychologists of the 20th century, typically ranked in the top 100; this monograph is a comprehensive and extensive documentation of his and others’ social psychology experiments through roughly the 1940–30197056yas, and is likewise widely cited. This ‘enlarged edition’ published 10 years later includes a new epilogue, which covers such topics as the 196858ya ‘Pygmalion Experiment’ (pg461, “The External Validity of Interpersonal Expectancy Effects”) While dryly written and often extremely technical, some parts of it are much easier and more interesting to read. Rosenthal begins by outlining examples of experimenter bias from areas like astronomy or biology: beyond well-known examples like N rays, because scientists often record data in manual fashion, they can be shown to bias their recorded values towards what they think is the right value and which they expect. Similarly, animals can react to their experimenters, as most famously demonstrated by the case of Clever Hans (the book on which I recommend for the sheer thoroughness and explication of how exactly Clever Hans did it). Rosenthal generalizes this to everything: individual experimenters elicit varying responses and also their demographic traits like sex or politics or personality traits, the room, the method of recording data (eg. paper-and-pencil vs interviewer vs camera), the experimental subjects’ own expectations and individual differences, expectancies driven by data snooping/early returns (potentially leading to self-fulfilling prophecies through positive feedback loops), etc. Rosenthal is no doomsayer, however, and is interested in solutions. Expectancy effects can be controlled by appropriate use of multiple interviews/experimenters, inducing effects, rendered consistent or removed entirely by using indirect instruments like computers, and so on; Rosenthal provides a number of statistical power analyses to help with estimating n/k values, as well as proposing new approaches like ‘result-blind peer review’ (intended to reduce publication bias by journals/reviewers by hiding the final results, and forcing them to evaluate the methodology and hypothesis & data on its own merits). I acquired a copy primarily for chapter 3, “Intentional Error”, where Rosenthal is the first known person to suggest a kind of ‘result-blind peer review’ to avoid ‘file drawer effect’/publication bias by having results removed from submitted articles and publication decided based solely on the methods/design. (He may not be the absolute first person, since I’ve found something like 10 ‘multiple discoveries’ of the idea, but he currently holds the record.) Rosenthal also made many contributions to early practice of meta-analysis and discussion of publication bias. The final chapter in this second edition excitedly reports results from their latest experiment, demonstrating social expectancy effects by telling teachers that some of their students were considerably more intelligent than their grades indicated, and they should have higher expectations of those students; the targeted students showed IQ gains measured before/after. This appendix is immediately recognizable as… the ‘Pygmalion effect’. This chapter was like “the thirteenth stroke of a crazy clock, which discredits not only itself, but all that went before”; the scales immediately fell from my eyes. I had somehow forgotten that Rosenthal was the originator of the now-infamous ‘Pygmalion effect’. As Jussim and Harber 2005 covers, the Pygmalion effect was conceived in sin, borne of ideology, clothed with deception, and nourished on naivete while unnaturally prolonging its undead life. The original ‘Pygmalion effect’ research paper turned out to be driven by a level of ostensible incompetence indistinguishable from idiocy or ideology. The supposed IQ gains (in just a few subsets) stem entirely from a few datapoints where the pupil in question went from an IQ indicative of clinical retardation before the mindset intervention, to genius afterwards; when those are removed, the ‘Pygmalion effect’ effects a disappearance. It is as if Rosenthal et al had measured the heights of the students, placidly recorded that the student body included a few 1-foot-tall students, instructed the teachers in a memo to think more elevated thoughts, and returned to measure the now-8-foot-tall students—concluding they had discovered a marvelously effective and scalable intervention for literally boosting students up, surely worthy of further in-depth study… (The specific IQ data points, according to Snow 1995 on obtaining the original raw data from Rosenthal: 17 → 110 (+93), 18 → 122 (+104), 133 → 202 (+69), 111 → 208 (+97), & 113 → 211 (+98)! One can commend Rosenthal only for not resorting to the usual researcher excuses like ‘privacy’ or ‘the dog ate their homework’ to cover this up.) Naturally, of course, all the teachers who believed Rosenthal, much like they still believe in “multiple intelligences” and whole-word reading, immediately saw half their classes turn into geniuses who excelled academically with their eyes closed, singlehandedly boosting the national IQ and rendering the Flynn effect irrelevant in the face of the almighty Pygmalion effect—oh wait, nothing like that ever happened, and no matter how widely the news spread or how teachers acted, they got the same results they did every year, and every subsequent study tended to turn in slightly smaller effects. Huh. Rosenthal then began defending using statistical gimmicks like the “fail-safe n” for meta-analysis, which estimates the number of studies generated by a null hypothesis of zero effect which is necessary to ‘dilute’ the Pygmalion effect to non-statistical-significance, and turns in reassuringly-large numbers like hundreds or thousands of studies; the argument being that there could not possibly be that many Pygmalion effect studies hidden away in file drawers and thus the effect has to be real—except that’s not how publication bias or p-hacking works! Studies don’t get published at random, and the entire point of publication bias is that only the studies that come out ‘right’ will be published. Regardless of his statistical gimmickry, the hundreds of attempts to replicate the Pygmalion effect showed some of the most striking ‘decline effects’ around, where, as time passed and methodology improved and non-Rosenthal-affiliated experimenters (who assume it’s real) ran experiments, the gains of scores of IQ points shrank to slivers of points (similar to recent fads for “growth mindset”), fading into the ‘crud factor’. Now, the Pygmalion effect lives a vampiric existence: undead and unkillable by mere mortals’ evidence, it rises at night to drain the life of researchers who must answer questions from educators and laymen about how “doesn’t the Pygmalion effect prove IQ is easily increased?” or “how can IQ tests have any validity or predictive power if they are so powerfully affected by expectancy effects (as proven by Rosenthal)?” Then there’s Tryon’s Rat Experiment, where Rosenthal supposedly replicated the results on breeding ‘maze-bright’ rats by instructing students handling rats which rats were ‘maze-bright’ and not, without any genetics involved, thus demonstrating, per Pavlov, that “the apparent improvement in the ability to learn, on the part of successive generations of mice, was really due to an improvement in the ability to teach, on the part of the experimenter” (Rosenthal and Fode 1963/pg175). And yet, if you read Tryon, this could not have been the case because he spent enormous efforts beginning in the 1920s on building a remarkable mechanical maze to improve measurement and remove any bias! Rosenthal never mentions this in the paper/book, despite it being relevant to his sections on the desirability of automating measurement as much as possible. Reading this made me so angry I was unable to review it for 3 years. Rosenthal exemplifies the Replication Crisis. Rarely have such gifts been so misapplied and thought so corrupted. The irony of this book is that Rosenthal lucidly describes the sins of researchers in p-hacking their results, being underpowered, letting their expectations guide their analysis and data collection, the need for replication, solutions for various biases—and then proceeds to use it as a checklist. Everything in this book is untrustworthy; perhaps a quarter of the results might be real (albeit much smaller than claimed), but there is no way to know what wine has been mixed together with the sewage. (As Meehl notes, most psychology theories never get debunked, they just fade away. If you don’t replicate a result, well then, you must’ve worn the wrong color sweater that day—those darn experimenter effects.) As Meehl and Cohen have observed, I believe, the current Replication Crisis is far from the first one in psychology. (In fact, the psychology practice of publishing multiple confirmatory studies in a single paper—which Schimmack has exploited to develop his ‘incredibility index’ quantifying how impossible it is for all studies in a paper to turn out statistically-significant and confirming the claims—was itself a methodological response to an earlier crisis.) Who can read through the Pygmalion effect debate, or Experimenter Expectancy Effects as a whole, and not recognize the same damn things? Mouse Utopia, Robber’s Cave, stereotype threat, willpower/ego depletion, the bystander effect, Zimbardo’s Stanford Prison Experiment, the backfire effect—the whole rotten crew wouldn’t miss a beat if dropped into the pages of EEE. Nor is it so hard to guess what Rosenthal’s expectancies here are. You don’t need to read Duarte et al 2015 to guess where Rosenthal’s allegiances lie, and why he is so invested in the Pygmalion effect or the idea that there exist innumerable environmental influences molding every aspect of human existence, to which invisible puppet strings we dance, or the policy implications. Even if perhaps the (homeopathically-small) data from any given experiment aren’t quite 100% rigorous, surely the conclusions are “justified by the important message he is trying to send”? Worse, it is that most insidious of books—not just occasionally but systematically wrong from start to finish, and it appears extraordinarily rigorous; the more one learns from this book, the more wrong one becomes. (A badly brilliant book like Atlas Shrugged can be droll, but a brilliantly bad book is deadly.) How should anyone know this without the benefit of enormous amounts of hindsight, like knowledge of how the Pygmalion effect turned out or having witnessed the current Replication Crisis? After all, the studies appear to be repeatedly replicated and confirmed; Rosenthal can pull out of his hat all sort of studies conducted by his students or associates or associates on students (often unpublished or selectively published in the paper vs book version, implying huge levels of publication bias at every phase), and—mirabile dictu—the endless ANOVAs and t-tests almost all turn in the critical p < 0.05 (despite tiny n), and when they don’t, well, the p-value is trending towards statistical-significance anyway. This is possible because all of the effects are large. Somehow, many of these manipulations and effects manage to reach large values, like r = 0.3 or d = 0.5 which puts them in the range of statistical-significance with their available n. And yet, isn’t that an absurd view of human psychology? If we have an r = 0.3 from adding the specific experimenter as an effect, that’s another way of saying R2=10% variance is explainable by that variable. So if I collect another 9 of these expectancy effects—the room size, the interviewer’s sweater color, the time of day, the brand of pencil, who the subject walked by on the way to the interview room and their demographics—I would approach 100% variance explained and perfect prediction? How does that work, exactly…? It’s the ‘piranha problem’ (Tosh et al 2021): how can we have all of these supposedly large effects from mere exposure to a prime or media when we are super-saturated by environmental stimuli? How do we reconcile these claims that IQs can be enormously modified by a teacher, in just a few minutes of interaction a day, for a school year, with the long-term stability from, say, age ~11 to age 70+ in the Scottish sample after exposure to thousands of people over a lifetime? How, indeed, do we reconcile it with the fact that we can recognize the same person from day to day? How is anything we observe in the world consistent with Rosenthal’s expectancy results if we take them literally? These facts poke, per Bates Yet more holes in the idea that human psychology flutters in a breeze of trivial situations, like a tired butterfly. There cannot be these reams of manipulable everyday powerful variables, and Rosenthal’s ability to find them and spend 470 pages discussing them discredits him, them, and the paradigm as a whole, much like how psi researchers’ ability to keep finding evidence of psi demonstrates that standard psychological methods are (just as Rosenthal argues) too weak to stop motivated researchers from finding what they want. Many people are sensible enough to know that psi doesn’t exist, no matter how many p-values are piled up; but Rosenthal’s nonsense, unfortunately, suits their nonsense. I do not recommend this book. I do not recommend reading it. I do not recommend believing anything in it. It is one of the most insanely idiotic books I have read, and at no point approaches anything which could be considered clearly not a false positive or grossly overestimated; everyone is dumber for it existing. I award it 0 stars and may God have mercy on its author’s soul.

title: 100 Years of Nobel Prizes

mentions.title: 100 Years of Nobel Prizes
mentions.context: 100 Years of Nobel Prizes, Shalev 2002 100 Years of Nobel PrizesBaruch A. Shalev2002★☆☆☆☆ A compilation of Nobel Prize winners up to 200323ya. Oddly, this book is cited on Wikipedia, and I took a look at a copy. It is a very short book, and largely devoid of any value in studying the Nobel Prize, consisting mostly of just raw summary statistics and graphs slicing prizes by various demographics. What value it has is reduced by being now 15 years out of date, which now is equivalent to a fifth of its sample. The 2 main problems with it are that it is totally silent about sources or methods, and that its statistical analysis never rises above the rudimentary. The lack of sourcing or discussion of methodology means that its claims typically either are trivial (prize winners by country, gender, or field; data easily obtained from the Nobel Prize website or other sources, yielding the obvious results like USA/UK and males dominating), or cannot be trusted because no details are provided about where data came from or what definitions are used even in areas where the results can be expected to be strongly influenced by the details. What is true in it is not new, and what is new may not be true. The main example of the latter is its breakdown of religion: It includes a remarkably fine-grained breakdown of prizes by religion (mostly Christian or Jewish, of course), including a chart for ‘percentage of Total Nobel Prizes won by Atheists, Agnostics, and Freethinkers between 1901–99200026ya’. One might expect the percentages to be quite high, but they are low, <10% for everything but Literature, with the most theistic fields apparently being Peace and physics (4.7%). Considering the correlation of atheism with intelligence, reports of extreme irreligion among elite scientists (in anonymous surveys and profiles, like Anne Roe’s study of anonymized Nobel-level scientists whose religion section is perhaps 2 pages long and notes simply “that aspect of life just does not exist for them”), and that atheists are one of the most hated and discriminated against minorities, even now after a century of increasing acceptance, with surveys attempting to correct for self-protection finding much higher rates of atheism (a very recent example using Bayesian truth serum-style techniques to increase atheism estimates by 2-7×: Gervais and Najle 2017), the results are questionable, and in some respects defy belief—we are supposed to believe that Nobel-level physicists are 5 times less likely to be atheist than the general population, and much less likely than chemistry/medicine/literature Nobelists? It’s not as if Nobelists are not under considerable pressure to be prestigious and orthodox—if you believe their public statements, Nobelists are less likely than the general population to use psychedelic drugs (as only 3 rather iconoclastic Nobelists have admitted to it—Feynman, possibly Crick, & Mullis—while a good 10% of the American population has used psychedelic drugs at some point), Richard Feynman felt constricted by being a Nobelist, and another Richard, Hamming, who knew Nobelists, observes that winning the Nobel seems to have something of a paralytic effect: [Hamming on the ‘Nobel Prize effect’] While one doesn’t expect a rigorous anonymous survey which might reveal true beliefs rather than little white lies for public consumption (surveying Nobelists being difficult in the best of times, much less a century later), it is still important for interpretation to understand where these numbers are coming from and to what extent they are skewed by PR or obfuscation like Albert Einstein. (Perhaps they are “spiritual but not religious”…) However, in explaining where these figures come from, the sole mention in the book appears to be: A review of the Nobel awards between 1901125ya and 200026ya reveals that 654 Laureates belong to 28 different religions. Most (65.4%) have identified Christianity in its various forms as their religious preference. While separating Roman Catholic from Protestants among Christians proved difficult in some cases, available information suggests that more Protestants were involved in the scientific categories and more Catholics were involved in the Literature and Peace categories. Oh. Of course. ‘A review’. Naturally. How could one doubt that? Such glibness is all the more infuriating in a book-length treatment of a topic which allows for, and ought to go into far more detail than a paper (not that such silence on how the data was created would be remotely acceptable in a paper either!). Further rubbing salt into the wound, the book blandly refers the reader for the dataset to a… CD-ROM. Which they have to pay for, again, quite a bit of money: A CD-ROM containing all the data in the book is available for separate purchase for $40.96$21.952002. It allows users to sort Nobel information by name, year, sex, country, institution, nationality, religion, and so on. In addition, users can obtain full information on each laureate and country if desired. For information on acquiring the CD-ROM, please communicate with the publisher as follows: Not that I expect there are any CD-ROMs sitting around the publisher’s offices ~16 years later (or that they would be readable). As opposed to printing the dataset in a table over 10 or 20 pages, or, let’s go totally crazy here, he could have put a 1MB spreadsheet on this exciting new thing they had back in 200323ya called “the Internet”. For that matter, how were variables like “country of origin” or time of work estimated? (Bueller? Bueller?) Sprinkled throughout are errors that undermine faith in the work, like praising Einstein’s work on “antigravity” (I think this is supposed to refer to the cosmological constant), or remarking on the longevity of Nobelists (well, yes, aside from the known causal influence of education/intelligence/SES on longevity, Nobelists will inherently be long-lived because they aren’t awarded posthumously!), or a particularly ignorant remark suggesting that Jewish persecution and the Holocaust has made them a genetically superior race and this explains their overrepresentation among Nobelists (which doesn’t explain why Jewish achievement has not substantially increased post-WWII, was so high in the USA where they were treated far better than elsewhere, doesn’t explain why a process as random and destructive to upper classes/intellectuals as the Holocaust would be expected to be a highly accurate selection for intelligence, and doesn’t work quantitatively anyway even under the most favorable estimate of truncation selection—and why is a supposed professional geneticist unable to do this back-of-the-napkin estimate and realize it can’t work?). One can at least have a little more faith in the sourcing for the section on astrological sign of Nobelists, as birth date is hard to screw up. (Instead one is left asking—why on earth?) The analysis never rises above crude tabulation. This is striking as the topic clearly requires more sophisticated analysis. Without any clear theory or model, it doesn’t amount to much more than correlating, say, chocolate consumption with Nobelists. The numbers of Nobelists is absolutely small (719 prizes total, with duplicates, organizations winning etc.), and slicing by all the demographic variables, the number per cell quickly reaches zero. The sampling error must be severe and indicates many of these comparisons are illusory. A number of the prizes are bogus: he notes a number of prizes where the result was false, the Peace Prize is notoriously politicized and unreflective of achievements (eg. Obama’s Peace Prize), and the Literature Prize massively biased towards Scandinavians (although he doesn’t note that and instead chastises the Nobel Prize Committee for not awarding the Literature Prize to Scandinavian children’s authors like Astrid Lindgren!). Aside from biases in the process, many prizes which should have been awarded were not due to deaths, producing a longevity bias, one which is steadily worsening as the lags between work and achievement continually increase. On top of this, there are strong temporal trends, massive increases in global & scientific populations. All of these interact: for example, he notes that East Asia and Israel perform poorly but fails to realize that at least part of this is simply that they have done Nobel-level work but the increasing multi-decade lags means they simply haven’t gotten the prizes yet, and indeed, we have recently seem more Nobels going to those countries (eg. the anti-malaria 201511ya Nobel in Medicine to a Chinese researcher for work back in 1972, 43 years before). A better study of Nobel Prizes would have to do a lot more work than slapping down some spreadsheet crosstabulations and calling it a day. A particularly valuable contribution would be to go through the Nobel archives and look at nominations and researchers who didn’t win (“Close but no Nobel: the scientists who never won; Archives reveal the most-nominated researchers who missed out on a Nobel Prize”); this would allow measurement of the extent to which Nobels are mistakenly awarded or influenced by chance, causing measurement error, and replacing a very crude dichotomized extremized measure (a few hundred winners vs everyone else) of just a few datapoints with a continuous one of many (thousands of researchers by number of nominations) which is less susceptible to longevity bias and allows direct incorporation of right-censoring. Comparison of winners with nominees adds considerable causal credibility to inferences; for example, the longevity bias means it’s not obvious if winning increases longevity, but what you can do is compare winners to almost-winners, arguing it’s like a regression-discontinuity design, and Rablen and Oswald 2008 do just that and still find a (smaller) longevity boost. The increasing lag times should also be included to avoid a systematic bias against recent changes in scientific accomplishment (eg. the rise of East Asia). It would be very justifiable to exclude Nobelists who we know now were wrong or harmful (eg. lobotomy), and model in the biases like the pro-Scandinavian-writer bias in the Literature Prize (the Literature Prize is so unreliable they had to stop awarding it recently due to scandal). And so on. In general, the issues involved in using Nobels as a proxy for scientific accomplishment or national IQ are serious enough that I am not a big fan of invoking Nobel tallies unless absolutely necessary, and this book makes no serious effort to do so. An example of a better, or at least more interesting, result would be papers like Jones and Weinberg 2011. I do not recommend this book. There must be better sources on the Nobel Prize.

title: The Complete Poems
author: Randall Jarrell

mentions.title: The Complete Poems
mentions.context: The Complete Poems, Jarrell 1981 The Complete PoemsRandall Jarrell1981★☆☆☆☆ 491 pages, ~263 poems. Randall Jarrell followed a typically academic career for 20th century American poet, bouncing through various universities and nonprofit/government positions until his early death; he is often cited and quoted for his critical opinions and 1 WWII poem (some of which are quite good and I fully agree with), but his actual poetry is rarely quoted and hardly available online. So when a quotation of the ending of his poem “A Ghost, A Real Ghost” intrigued me, I had to get a used copy to see the rest of it. It was overall a bust and I struggled to finish it. Jarrell turns out to be a far greater literary critic than poet. I usually consider a collection of poetry a success if I like even a few poems in it, but despite plowing through several hundred often very long poems of his, I have to consider it appallingly dreary at best. Jarrell’s style is the worst of the 20th century academic style (doubtless he played a role in creating it), free verse in turgid ponderous descriptions, abounding with endless rhetorical questions and pathetic fallacies invoking abstractions. (Not for the first time I wonder why English 20th century is so systematically and totally appalling.) There is no music to his verse, and he is trapped in his own style—the only time his poems come anywhere near conveying anything is when the topic matter is so searing it overcomes his mannerisms (some of the WWII poems) or when formal considerations or imitation/parody force him out of his chosen shackles and into another voice. The last two categories are particularly sad because it’s clear that Jarrell did have literary talent, from how easily and lightly he rhymes and mimicks, but had too much freedom and lapsed into mediocrity. No T.S. Eliot, the few good lines of “A Girl in a Library” are buried in a tedious mass of pages and overintellectualizing, and likewise “A Ghost, A Real Ghost” is in bad need of a rewrite to make the first half stand up to the second half. In a more dogmatic time, perhaps Jarrell would’ve been forced to be the poet he could’ve been. A few poems: “A Ghost, a Real Ghost”: I think of that old woman in the song Who could not know herself without the skirt They cut off while she slept beside a stile. Her dog jumped at the unaccustomed legs And barked till she turned slowly from her gate And went—I never asked them where she went. The child is hopeful and unhappy in a world Whose future is his recourse: she kept walking Until the skirt grew, cleared her head and dog— Surely I thought so when I laughed. If skirts don’t grow, If things can happen so, and you not know What you could do, why, what is there you could do? I know now she went nowhere; went to wait In the bare night of the fields, to whisper: “I’ll sit and wish that it was never so.” I see her sitting on the ground and wishing, The wind jumps like a dog against her legs, And she keeps thinking: “This is all a dream.” “Who would cut off a poor old woman’s skirt? So good too. No, it’s not so: No one could feel so, really.” And yet one might. A ghost must; and she was, perhaps, a ghost. The first night I looked into the mirror And saw the room empty, I could not believe That it was possible to keep existing In such pain: I have existed. Was the old woman dead? What does it matter? —Am I dead? A ghost, a real ghost Has no need to die: what is he except A being without access to the universe That he has not yet managed to forget? –pg262–263, The Complete Poems (originally The Woman at the Washington Zoo) “The Archangels’ Song” (from Goethe’s Faust) RAPHAEL: The sun sings out, as of old Against the spheres’ unchanging sound; Yet once more, with thunderous footsteps, He works out his predestined round. Though no angel fathoms him, his face Gives strength to them upon their way; The inconceivably exalted works Are glorious as on the first day. GABRIEL: Swift, past all understanding swift Is the splendor of earth’s whirling flight: The brilliance of Paradise is changed For the awful darkness of the night. The ocean foams up, overwhelming, The great rocks tremble with the force, And rocks and ocean are swept onward In the spheres’ swift, eternal course. MICHAEL: In rivalry the tempests roar From sea to land, from land to sea, And, raging, forge out for the earth Fetters of wildest energy. Before the path of the thunderbolt The lightnings of desolation blaze. And yet thine angels, Lord, adore The tranquil footsteps of thy days. ALL THREE: Since none can fathom thee, thy face Gives strength to us upon our way, And thine exalted works, O God, Are glorious as on the first day. –pg251–252 “Song: Not There” I went to the cupboard, I opened the door, I cried to my people, O it’s not there! “How long did you think it would last?” said the cook, Said the butler, “Does anyone care?” But where is it, where is it? O it’s not there, Not there to be saved, not there to be saved If I’m saved it will not be there. I ran to a plate, to a pig, to a dish, An old china pig, a plate, to a pear, Said, To find it, O, I will look anywhere, Said, Anywhere, Anywhere… “Look anywhere,” Said the plate as it laughed, “yes, look anywhere; There’s as good as here, there’s as good as there— For where shall you look to be saved?” I said to my people, the plate, to the cupboard, The pig on its platter, the pear, the pear: O where is my salvation “O it’s not anywhere. You break in my head like a dish”, said the plate, “A pig”, said the pig, “a pear”, said the pear— Not there to be saved, go not there to be saved, If you’re saved it will not be there. –pg105 “The Owl’s Bedtime Story” There was once upon a time a little owl. He lived with his mother in a hollow tree. On winter nights he’d hear the foxes howl, He’d hear his mother call, and he would see The moonlight glittering upon the snow: How many times he wished for company As he sat there alone! He’d stand on tiptoe, Staring across the forest for his mother, And hear her far away; he’d look below And see the rabbits playing with each other And see the ducks together on the lake And wish that he’d a sister or a brother: Sometimes it seemed to him his heart would break. The hours went by, slow, dreary, wearisome, And he would watch, and sleep a while, and wake— “Come home! Come home!” he’d think; and she would come At last, and bring him food, and they would sleep. Outside the day glared, and the troublesome Sounds of the light, the shouts and caws that keep An owl awake, went on; and, dark in daylight, The owl and owlet nestled there. But one day, deep In his dark dream, warm, still, he saw a white Bird flying to him over the white good. The great owl’s wings were wide, his beak was bright. He whispered to the owlet: “You have been good A long time now, and waited all alone Night after long night. We have understood And you shall have a sister of your own A friend to play with, if, now, you will fly From your warn nest into the harsh unknown World the sun lights.” Down from the bright sky The light fell, when at last the owlet woke. Far, far away he heard an owlet cry. The sunlight blazed upon a broken oak Over the lake, and as he saw the tree It seemed to the owlet that the sunlight spoke. He heard it whisper: “Come to me! O come to me!” The world outside was cold and hard and bare; But at last the owlet, flapping desperately, Flung himself out upon the naked air And lurched and staggered to the nearest limb Of the next tree. How good it felt to him, That solid branch! And, there in that green pine, How calm it was, how shadowy and dim! But once again he flapped into the sunshine— Through all the tumult of the unfriendly day, Tree by tree by tree, along the shoreline Of the white lake, he made his clumsy way. At the bottom of the oak he saw a dead Owl in the snow. He flew to where it lay All cold and still; he looked at it in dread. Then something gave a miserable cry— There in the oak’s nest, far above his head, An owlet sat. He thought: The nest’s too high, I’ll never reach it. “Come here!” he called. “Come here!” But the owlet hid. And so he had to try To fly up—and at last, when he was near And stopped, all panting, underneath the nest And she gazed down at him, her face looked dear As his own sister’s, it was the happiest Hour of his life. In a little, when the two Had made friends, they started home. He did his best To help her: lurching and staggering, she flew From branch to branch, and he flapped at her side. The sun shone, dogs barked, boys shouted—on they flew. Sometimes they’d rest; sometimes they would glide A long way, from a high tree to a low, So smoothly—and they’d feel so satisfied, So grown-up! Then, all black against the snow, Some crows came cawing, ugly things! The wise Owlets sat still as mice; when one big crow Sailed by, a branch away, they shut their eyes And looked like lumps of snow. And when the night, The friend of owls, had come, they saw the moon rise And there came flying to them through the moonlight The mother owl. How strong, how good, how dear She did look! “Mother!” they called in their delight. Then the three sat there just as we sit here, And nestled close, and talked—at last they flew Home to the nest. All night the mother would appear And disappear, with good things; and the two Would eat and eat and eat, and then they’d play. But when the mother came, the mother knew How tired they were. “Soon it will be day And time for every owl to be in his nest”, She said to them tenderly; and they Felt they were tired, and went to her to rest. She opened her wings, they nestled to her breast. –pg348–350

title: Left In The Dark
author: Tony Wright and Graham Gynn

mentions.title: Left In The Dark
mentions.context: Left In The Dark, Gynn 2008 Left in the dark: the biological origins of the fall from grace: an investigation into the evolution of the human brain: a journey to the edge of the human mindGraham Gynn2008★☆☆☆☆ Having seen an overview of the claims, I expected little from this book but I was hopeful that it could at least be “mind candy” in the same sense that I enjoyed tremendously reading Jayne’s Origin of Consciousness in the Breakdown of the Bicameral Mind. But having finished reading it, I’m disappointed. It’s not fit to shine Jaynes’s boot buckle; while Jaynes’s theory has serious problems (explaining where bicameralism went, worldwide, and other chronological problems, for starters), it at least was an elegant theory that fit a great many facts! Wright and his co-author, on the other hand, is chock-full of anecdotes (better ping-pong playing and relaxation playing with your left hand? really?); data seems misrepresented (I did not recognize his description of the peg data in the sleep deprivation experiment with the actual graph); dismissal of possibilities as ‘implausible’ which are perfectly plausible (the claim that testosterone can’t damage one hemisphere and help the other comes to mind, as does the claim that there are no plausible evolutionary theories for evolving handedness—actually, there’s an elegant competition explanation with empirical support which anyone who has done a head-to-head sport like ping-pong or fencing could appreciate…); fully general counter-arguments like the claim that not appreciating the theory is evidence of being damaged as the theory predicts; excuse-making for the absence of forest fossils supporting their theory; blatantly false claims about bipedalism mixed in with distraction about the aquatic ape theory; claims about agricultural longevity which are surely the elementary mistake of assuming that infant mortality-dominated average lifespans say much about how adults actually lived; invocation of pseudoscience like photoreading or Carlos Castaneda or 140-year olds in distant Third World countries (seriously? seriously‽) or Alzheimer’s and other diseases being caused by dehydration; blatant confirmation bias† (who, interested in people who do not sleep, would mention a Vietnamese woman and not mention fatal familial insomnia?); and of course, vitamin C megadoses must appear in any work by fruitarians, as does the claim that cooking reduces the nutritional value of food (which would come as news to anthropologists, who regard the introduction of fire as possibly the key breakthrough to enabling large expensive brains—except that right, the authors believe that fruit is what enabled large brains, well, I wonder why they might not discuss the caloric value of cooking food… perhaps it’s because cooked food doesn’t ‘raise micro-electric potentials throughout the body’). † which becomes ever more important in data-rich noisy fields like psychology; I actually pointed this out for dual n-back recently on Hacker News and more generally in my Replication Crisis page The use of autists, idiot savants, and TMS is an interesting topic in its own right, but inadvertently sabotages the thesis. There’s a legal saying, ‘hard cases make bad law’; in neuroscience, damaged patients make bad theories. The brain is Turing-complete and can exhibit arbitrarily complex problems: these patients tend to be fairly unique, and how are you going to build any kind of theory on them? To the extent we can infer anything, it’s that there is a common trait among those with access to low-level processing: they are not smart. Their abilities seem to come at the expense of all other abilities or higher-level processing: Kim Peek may have memorized thousands of books, but what sort of understanding did this man with an IQ of 89 exhibit of them? Very little. The child prodigy artist may be able to render remarkably detailed artwork, but a camera is more accurate and just as artistic as I’ve ever heard him be. This does not bode well for any exaltation of the right hemisphere… The crowning piece of nonsense is probably the ‘loop’ between fruits, steroids, and DNA. This idea, lovingly illustrated in multiple graphs, is fractal nonsense: the more you look at each piece, the worse it gets. It’s as if someone told you that car evolution was steered by gas stations: you see, a human drives the car to a gas station, the car is filled up with gas, the gas changes the car, changing how it drives to the next gas station and how it reacts to the next fill-up. This may initially seem plausible until you look at step 3, which reads basically like the old Far Side strip—‘And then a miracle occurs’. How exactly do steroids rewrite the DNA? A steroid is not a little computer or nanobot which can go into a sperm or egg—and notice the quiet eliding of the difference between somatic and germ-line cells, it’s perfectly possible for any genetic or epigenetic changes to not be passed on—and rewrite the DNA as it wishes. If variations in circulating levels of some chemical affect DNA, it must do so via receptors and proteins set up in advance by gradual evolution to do specific things—eg. think of how alligators or crocodiles vary the sex ratio of their offspring in response to ambient temperatures, this is set up in advance because it’s useful, the temperature doesn’t ‘just cause’ the sex ratio to vary in some magical way because boy alligators are fiery and analogous to hot weather while female crocodiles are chillier and aloof. (I’m reminded of the genie of the lamp: “I wish everyone was happy!” Well, OK, but what does that actually mean and how should the genie do it?) They are, naturally, as sure of this evolutionary loop as one can be in the complete absence of all evidence. While we’re on DNA, I was deeply amused that they could propose this system as their primary explanation, and then throughout the rest of the book dismiss any further adaptation because a few hundred thousand years was not enough! I really think that we can adapt to eating meat in a few hundred thousand years, especially when our primate ancestors and surviving lineages often do eat meat… It was especially funny to read “It is highly unlikely that the DNA selection process could have achieved this rapid result (certainly not on the savanna where hominids would be subjected to hard and stressful environmental conditions)”; hard and stressful conditions are exactly the kind of selection pressure that might drive large increases in any organ or body part, and allometric scaling in general is one of the easier things for evolution to change if it’s fitness-increasing. (Changing size is a lot easier than developing an organ from scratch, that’s for sure. Size is a tweak.) These are only my notes for the first 80 pages. After that, I gave up and read on in a sort of stunned state. At least it does deign to include some sort of references (although it doesn’t link specific claims to specific papers, seems kind of skimpy, and is very heavy on books—which aren’t very useful in the sense that now you have an entire book to read just to check a few claims). It helps that I’ve read up on many of the same topics for entirely different reasons, so I have a good idea of the general framework of various fields and where they’re making huge extrapolations or passing over contrary evidence. ‘What is good in it is not original, and what is original is not good.’ The disturbing thing for me is that so many of the references and facts are familiar, and it’s written fairly well. I’m reminded of an apocryphal quote (usually attributed to Anatole France): What frightens us most in a madman is his sane conversation.

title: Far Side
author: Gary Larson

mentions.title: Far Side
mentions.context: The crowning piece of nonsense is probably the ‘loop’ between fruits, steroids, and DNA. This idea, lovingly illustrated in multiple graphs, is fractal nonsense: the more you look at each piece, the worse it gets. It’s as if someone told you that car evolution was steered by gas stations: you see, a human drives the car to a gas station, the car is filled up with gas, the gas changes the car, changing how it drives to the next gas station and how it reacts to the next fill-up. This may initially seem plausible until you look at step 3, which reads basically like the old Far Side strip—‘And then a miracle occurs’. How exactly do steroids rewrite the DNA? A steroid is not a little computer or nanobot which can go into a sperm or egg—and notice the quiet eliding of the difference between somatic and germ-line cells, it’s perfectly possible for any genetic or epigenetic changes to not be passed on—and rewrite the DNA as it wishes. If variations in circulating levels of some chemical affect DNA, it must do so via receptors and proteins set up in advance by gradual evolution to do specific things—eg. think of how alligators or crocodiles vary the sex ratio of their offspring in response to ambient temperatures, this is set up in advance because it’s useful, the temperature doesn’t ‘just cause’ the sex ratio to vary in some magical way because boy alligators are fiery and analogous to hot weather while female crocodiles are chillier and aloof. (I’m reminded of the genie of the lamp: “I wish everyone was happy!” Well, OK, but what does that actually mean and how should the genie do it?) They are, naturally, as sure of this evolutionary loop as one can be in the complete absence of all evidence.
